prose.summary: Computational designers use code and parametric systems to generate, test or coordinate design options. In the current evidence, the role sits mainly around architecture, urban design and BIM. It is not simply a designer who knows a scripting language.
prose.day_to_day: The work combines geometry, rules, model data and design review. Designers build parametric definitions, automate repetitive modeling, test alternatives and connect outputs to BIM or documentation workflows. The live sample is very small and includes both specialist and internship titles. That makes the role look more like a practice-specific capability than a standardized occupation.
prose.work_environment: The available openings are site-based in Switzerland, with no remote roles in the sample. The work itself is computer-heavy, but close collaboration with architects, researchers and BIM teams keeps it tied to project studios. The sample is too small to generalize beyond those openings.
prose.getting_in: Start with design competence, then use Rhino, Grasshopper, Python or BIM tools to solve a real project problem. A useful portfolio shows the rule, inputs, alternatives and downstream output, not only a complex form. Candidates from architecture, BIM or design technology have the clearest adjacent route.
prose.ladder: Early work builds scripts and parametric studies under a project lead. Responsibility can grow toward reusable workflows, research, automation strategy and coordination between design and delivery systems. The path may branch into design technology, BIM management or advanced architectural practice.
prose.suits: This work suits people who enjoy design rules, geometry and repeated testing more than one-off manual production. It requires patience with debugging and willingness to make a method usable by colleagues. It is a poor fit if code is only a way to produce visual novelty.
prose.misconceptions: Computational design is not defined by unusual geometry. The stronger use is encoding a repeatable design or coordination problem so alternatives can be tested and delivered more consistently.
prose.who_qualifies: Architects, BIM specialists and design technologists bring the closest adjacent foundations. They need to prove parametric reasoning and enough coding to maintain their own workflow. A software background without design judgment leaves the opposite gap.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The live sample is too small to show a stable tool standard or seniority pattern. It also cannot reveal whether a studio treats computational work as core delivery or occasional visualization support.

steps.how: Pick a repeatable geometry, analysis or documentation task that manual production handles poorly.
Use Rhino, Grasshopper, Python or BIM tools to expose inputs, rules and predictable outputs.
Change the input range, break the definition and document what the workflow can and cannot handle.
Export useful model data, drawings or BIM content so the project does not end as a disconnected experiment.

prose.tools: Grasshopper, parametric design, Python and Rhino lead the small evidence sample, with ArchiCAD, BIM, Git and Revit also present. The durable capability is making a design rule explicit and maintainable rather than knowing one plugin.

pros: The role can remove repetitive work while expanding design options.
It connects design practice with code and systems thinking.
cons: The current market sample is very small and geographically narrow.
Custom workflows become maintenance burdens when nobody else understands them.

faq.q: how do you become a computational designer?
faq.a: Start with a real design problem and build a parametric workflow that produces a useful project output. Show rules, edge cases and delivery, not only a striking image.

faq.q: do computational designers need to code?
faq.a: Usually. Visual scripting can cover part of the work, but Python or another language helps when workflows need data handling, automation and maintenance.

faq.q: what is the difference between a computational designer and a BIM manager?
faq.a: A computational designer builds parametric and automated design methods, while a BIM manager governs models, standards and coordination across teams. The roles overlap in BIM automation.
